93278.q: Where does the dust go in a vacuum cleaner?
93278.e: The dust is collected in a dust bag or a container. When it is full, you empty it or change it.
93278.m: The dust ends up in the dust bag.

93279.e: An electric motor turns a fan that sucks in the air. That is why a vacuum cleaner needs electricity.
93279.m: A motor makes the vacuum cleaner suck.

93280.q: What did people clean the floor with before the vacuum cleaner existed?
a: A broom and a carpet beater
93280.e: In the past, people swept the floor with a broom. Carpets were hung up outside and the dust was beaten out of them.
93280.m: In the past, people cleaned with a broom and a carpet beater.

93281.q: Which country did Hubert Cecil Booth, who built a large vacuum cleaner in 1901, come from?
93281.e: Hubert Cecil Booth was an English engineer. His first vacuum cleaner was so big that it was pulled through the streets by horses.
93281.m: An early vacuum cleaner came from England.

93283.q: What do you need to clear off the floor before you vacuum?
93283.e: Otherwise small things like Lego bricks would be sucked up. They can get stuck in the vacuum cleaner.
93283.m: Before vacuuming, you tidy away small things.

93284.q: Why does a vacuum cleaner have a filter?
a: So the dust does not blow out again
93284.e: The air goes back out of the vacuum cleaner. The filter holds back the fine dust as it does.
93284.m: The filter keeps the dust inside the vacuum cleaner.

93285.q: What is a small cordless vacuum cleaner that you hold in your hand called?
93285.e: A handheld vacuum cleaner has a rechargeable battery instead of a cable. You use it to quickly suck up crumbs from the table or in the car.
93285.m: A handheld vacuum cleaner has a rechargeable battery.

93286.q: What is the part of the washing machine that turns with the washing called?
93286.e: The washing lies in a drum. The drum turns and moves the washing about in the water.
93286.m: The washing turns in the drum.

93287.q: What do you put in the washing machine to get the washing clean?
93287.e: Washing powder loosens dirt and stains. Together with water and movement, the washing gets clean.
93287.m: Washing powder makes the washing clean.

93288.q: What does the washing machine do during the spin cycle?
a: It turns fast and forces the water out
93288.e: During the spin, the drum turns very fast. This squeezes a lot of water out of the washing.
93288.m: During the spin, the water is flung out.

93289.q: What did people use to wash clothes by hand in the past?
93289.e: People rubbed the wet washing with soap on a ridged washboard. It was hard work.
93289.m: In the past, people washed on a washboard.

93290.q: What is the shared room for washing in many Swiss blocks of flats called?
93290.e: In many Swiss blocks of flats, everyone shares a laundry room. A washing rota sets out who may wash when.
93290.m: Many Swiss buildings have a shared laundry room.

93291.q: Why do you sort the washing before washing it?
a: So colour does not run onto light clothes
93291.e: New red or dark clothes can lose colour. A white T-shirt can then turn pink.
93291.m: Light and dark washing are washed separately.

93292.q: Which machine dries the washing with warm air after it has been washed?
93292.e: In Switzerland a tumble dryer is often just called a “Tumbler”. It turns the wet washing in warm air.
93292.m: The tumble dryer dries the washing.

93293.q: What does a label with a number in a tub of water on a piece of clothing show?
a: How hot you may wash it
93293.e: The symbol with the tub shows the highest washing temperature in degrees. If it says 30, you wash at 30 degrees at most.
93293.m: The label shows the washing temperature.

93294.q: What do you do with a toaster?
93294.e: In the toaster, slices of bread get hot. They turn brown and crispy.

93295.q: What gets hot in the toaster so that the bread toasts?
93295.e: There are heating wires in the toaster. The electricity makes them so hot that they glow red.

93296.q: What is the toasted bread from the toaster called?
93296.e: Bread that has been toasted is called toast. The German language has borrowed this word from English.

93297.q: What happens if you leave the bread in the toaster for too long?
93297.e: The longer the bread toasts, the darker it gets. In the end it burns and tastes bitter.
93297.m: Bread toasted for too long burns.

93298.q: What does a modern toaster do when the bread is ready?
93298.e: A spring pushes the bread up as soon as the time is up. The American Charles Strite invented this pop-up toaster around 1919.
93298.m: The toaster pops up the finished bread.

93299.q: Why must you never poke around in a toaster with a fork?
a: You can get an electric shock
93299.e: There are live wires inside the toaster. A metal fork conducts electricity, and that is dangerous.
93299.m: Metal does not belong in a toaster.

93300.q: What is the dial on many toasters for?
a: It sets how brown the bread gets
It chooses the type of bread
93300.e: With the dial you set the toasting time. A higher setting makes the bread darker.
93300.m: The dial decides how brown the toast gets.

93301.q: What collects at the bottom of the toaster and should be emptied now and then?
93301.e: When you toast, crumbs fall to the bottom. Many toasters have a crumb tray for them.

93302.q: What do you need a zip for?
93302.e: A zip closes jackets, trousers and bags in one pull. That is quicker than lots of buttons.

93303.q: What are the small parts of a zip that fit into each other called?
93303.e: A zip has two rows of small teeth. When you close it, they fit into each other like fingers.
93303.m: The teeth fit into each other.

93304.q: What is the part of a zip that you pull up and down called?
93304.e: The slider brings the teeth together or pulls them apart. It often has a small tab for pulling.
93304.m: You pull the slider up and down.

93305.q: What does the slider do when you close a zip?
a: It presses the teeth of both sides into each other
It glues the two sides together
It sews the two sides together
93305.e: The small teeth on both sides hook into each other. The slider brings them together so that they hold firmly.
93305.m: The slider fits the teeth of the zip into each other.

93306.q: What can the teeth of a zip be made of?
93306.e: On jeans, the teeth are often made of metal. On sports jackets, they are often made of plastic.
93306.m: Zips are made of metal or plastic.

93307.q: What did clothes often have instead of a zip, before zips existed?
93307.e: In the past, clothes were almost always fastened with buttons or hooks. Velcro and magnetic fasteners were invented much later.
93307.m: In the past, clothes mostly had buttons.

93308.q: Which zip comes completely apart at the bottom?
a: The one on a pair of trousers
The one on a pencil case
93308.e: On a jacket you can open the zip completely. That way you can take the jacket off like a coat.
93308.m: A jacket zip can be opened completely.

93309.q: What helps when a zip gets stuck?
a: Rubbing a pencil over the teeth
93309.e: The graphite rubbed off the pencil lead works like a lubricant. Then the slider glides more easily.
93309.m: Pencil graphite makes a zip run smoothly.

93310.q: What stops you pricking yourself on a safety pin?
93310.e: The point of the pin sits in a small cap. That way you do not prick yourself.

93311.q: What did Walter Hunt bend the first safety pin out of in 1849?
93311.e: The American Walter Hunt bent the safety pin out of a single piece of wire and had it protected by a patent in 1849.
93311.m: A safety pin is made of a bent wire.

93312.q: What is a safety pin bent out of?
93312.e: A safety pin is a piece of wire. It is bent into a spring, a pin and a clasp.
93312.m: A safety pin is made of wire.

93313.q: What does a safety pin have at the bend so that it springs back?
93313.e: At the bend, the wire is wound into a round loop. This spring presses the pin into the cap.
93313.m: A loop of wire makes the pin springy.

93314.q: What is a safety pin often used for in sport?
a: To pin on your race number
93314.e: In a race you wear a number on your shirt. It is fastened with safety pins.
93314.m: Race numbers are pinned on with safety pins.

93315.q: What can you quickly fix with a safety pin?
a: Trousers with a button torn off
93315.e: If a button is missing, a safety pin holds the fabric together. It is a quick emergency fix.
93315.m: A safety pin is good for quick repairs.

93316.q: What were safety pins often used for with babies in the past?
93316.e: In the past, babies had nappies made of cloth. A large safety pin held them together without pricking the baby.
93316.m: In the past, cloth nappies were fastened with safety pins.

93317.q: Why is the safety pin called that?
a: Because its point is safely covered
Because it is made of gold
93317.e: On a normal pin the point is free. On a safety pin it is covered, so it is safer.
93317.m: The safety pin hides its point.

93318.q: What do you need a paper clip for?
a: To hold sheets of paper together
93318.e: A paper clip holds a few sheets of paper together. You can take it off again without damaging the paper.
93318.m: A paper clip holds sheets together.

93319.q: What is a simple paper clip made of?
93319.e: A paper clip is a piece of wire bent into loops. The wire is springy and clamps the paper tight.
93319.m: A paper clip is a bent wire.

93320.q: What is the advantage of a paper clip compared with a stapler?
a: The paper does not get holes
93320.e: A stapler pushes staples through the paper. A paper clip only clamps it and leaves no holes.
93320.m: A paper clip makes no holes in the paper.

93321.q: How many sheets does a small paper clip hold together well?
93321.e: A small paper clip only clamps a few sheets. For lots of sheets you need a large clip or a folder.
93321.m: A small paper clip holds a few sheets.

93322.q: What happens if you keep bending a paper clip open and shut?
93322.e: When wire is bent back and forth many times, it gets tired at that spot. At some point it breaks there.
93322.m: Wire that is bent too often breaks.

93323.q: What fun thing can you make with lots of paper clips?
93323.e: Paper clips can be hooked into each other. This makes a long chain.
93323.m: Paper clips can be joined into a chain.

93324.q: What attracts a steel paper clip?
93324.e: Many paper clips are made of steel. Steel contains iron, and iron is attracted by a magnet.
93324.m: A magnet attracts steel paper clips.

93325.q: Where are paper clips often kept?
93325.e: Paper clips are small and easily get lost. That is why they are kept in a small box or tin.
93325.m: Paper clips are kept in a box.

93326.q: Roughly how long should you brush your teeth for?
93326.e: In two to three minutes you can clean all your teeth well. An egg timer or a song helps you keep time.
93326.m: Brushing your teeth takes about two to three minutes.

93327.q: After roughly how many months should you change your toothbrush?
93327.e: Over time the bristles get bent and clean less well. That is why you take a new one about every three months.
93327.m: You need a new toothbrush about every three months.

93328.q: What are the many fine hairs on a toothbrush called?
93328.e: The bristles rub the plaque off the teeth. Today they are mostly made of nylon, a type of plastic.
93328.m: The hairs of a toothbrush are called bristles.

93329.q: In which country were there toothbrushes with bristles more than 1000 years ago?
93329.e: In China, more than 1000 years ago, there were already brushes with a handle made of bamboo or bone. They are thought of as early toothbrushes.
93329.m: There was an early toothbrush in China.

93330.q: What were the bristles often made of in the past?
93330.e: In the past, people used stiff hairs from pigs. Nylon bristles have existed since about 1938.
93330.m: Toothbrushes used to be made with animal hair.

93331.q: What do you put on your toothbrush?
93331.e: Toothpaste helps with cleaning. It often contains fluoride, which strengthens the teeth.

93332.q: What does an electric toothbrush do by itself?
93332.e: A small motor turns or shakes the brush head. You just guide it from tooth to tooth.
93332.m: An electric toothbrush moves by itself.

93333.q: What is the lead of a pencil made of?
93333.e: Despite its name, there is no lead in a pencil. The lead is made of graphite and clay.
93333.m: There is no real lead in a pencil.

93334.q: What is the outer case of a wooden pencil usually made of?
93334.e: The lead sits in a case made of wood, often cedar. The wood is easy to sharpen.
93334.m: A pencil has a wooden case.

93335.q: What does HB on a pencil mean?
93335.e: H stands for hard and B for black, which means soft. An HB pencil lies right in between.
93335.m: HB stands for a medium hard pencil.

93336.q: What is the advantage of a pencil compared with a ballpoint pen?
a: You can rub out what you write
It writes in lots of colours
93336.e: Graphite only sits loosely on the paper. That is why you can remove it again with a rubber.
93336.m: Pencil writing can be rubbed out.

93337.q: What is the lead of a modern pencil made of?
93337.e: Despite its name, a pencil contains no lead. The lead is made of graphite mixed with clay. People used to think graphite was a kind of lead ore.
93337.m: Pencil leads are made of graphite and clay, not lead.

93338.q: What shape is a pencil often, so that it does not roll off the table?
93338.e: Many pencils have six edges. That way they do not roll away so easily and sit well in your hand.
93338.m: A hexagonal pencil does not roll away so easily.

93339.e: A rubber rubs the bits of graphite off the paper. That is how pencil marks disappear.
93339.m: A rubber gets rid of pencil marks.

93340.q: What were the first rubbers made from?
93340.e: The sap of the rubber tree turns into rubber. Around 1770, people noticed that it could rub out pencil.
93340.m: The first rubbers were made of tree sap.

93341.q: What did people use to rub out pencil before there were rubbers?
93341.e: In the past, people rubbed out pencil marks with soft bread. It worked, but it was crumbly.
93341.m: In the past, people rubbed things out with bread.

93342.q: What is left lying on the paper after rubbing out?
93342.e: When you rub, some rubber comes off. It rolls up with the graphite into small crumbs.

93343.q: Where is there a small rubber on some pencils?
a: In the middle of the wood
93343.e: Many pencils have a rubber at the end in a metal sleeve. This was already patented in 1858.
93343.m: Some pencils have a rubber at the top.

93344.q: Why can a normal rubber hardly remove ballpoint pen?
a: The ink soaks into the paper
93344.e: Ballpoint ink soaks into the paper fibres. Pencil, on the other hand, only stays on top of the paper.
93344.m: Ballpoint ink can hardly be rubbed out.

93345.q: What are most rubbers made of today?
93345.e: Today many rubbers are made of plastic such as vinyl. They rub out cleanly and smudge very little.
93345.m: Modern rubbers are made of plastic.

93346.q: Where does the word “erase” come from?
a: From a Latin word for scratching
From an English word for red
From a French word for bread
From an Italian word for rubber
93346.e: “Erase” comes from Latin and goes back to the word “radere”, which means to scratch or scrape. In the past, people scratched mistakes away with a knife.

93347.e: Tesa film is a thin, see-through tape with glue on one side. You use it to stick paper.
93347.m: Tesa film is a see-through sticky tape.

93348.q: On how many sides does normal sticky tape stick?
93348.e: Normal sticky tape only sticks on one side. But there is also double-sided tape.
93348.m: Normal sticky tape only sticks on one side.

93349.q: How is sticky tape usually stored?
93349.e: The tape is wound round a core. You pull off a piece and tear or cut it off.
93349.m: Sticky tape is wound onto a roll.

93350.q: What is sharp on a sticky tape dispenser?
93350.e: The dispenser has a jagged edge made of metal or plastic. You tear the tape off against it.
93350.m: You tear the tape off on the dispenser.

93351.q: In which German city did the company Beiersdorf bring out Tesa film in the 1930s?
93351.e: The company Beiersdorf from Hamburg brought out the see-through Tesa film in the 1930s. Later the name was used for many kinds of sticky tape.

93352.q: What do you often use to close wrapping paper when wrapping a present?
93352.e: A few strips of sticky tape hold the wrapping paper together. That way the present stays well wrapped.
93352.m: You stick wrapping paper down with sticky tape.

93353.q: What is sticky tape good for?
a: Mending a torn sheet of paper
93353.e: A tear in paper can be closed with a strip of sticky tape. Then the sheet holds together again.
93353.m: You mend paper with sticky tape.

93354.q: What is a wide brown tape for sealing cardboard boxes called?
93354.e: Parcel tape is wide and strong. You use it to seal boxes for a house move or for the post.
93354.m: Boxes are sealed with parcel tape.

93355.q: What often happens when you pull sticky tape off a poster on the wall?
a: A bit of paint or paper tears off with it
93355.e: The glue holds tight to the surface. When you pull it off, it can tear paint off the wall or paper with it.
93355.m: Sticky tape can tear things off when you pull it away.

93356.q: What is the part of the ear you can see on the outside of your head called?
93356.e: The outer ear is the part of the ear you can see. All the other parts are hidden inside the head.
93356.m: You can see the outer ear on the outside of your head.

93357.q: What is the outer ear for?
93357.e: The outer ear is shaped like a funnel. It collects sounds and guides them into the ear.
93357.m: The outer ear collects sounds like a funnel.

93358.q: What do people often do with their hand to hear better?
a: Hold it in front of the eyes
93358.e: A cupped hand behind the ear makes the outer ear bigger. That way it catches more sound.
93358.m: A hand behind the ear helps you hear.

93359.q: What is the soft lower part of the outer ear called?
93359.e: The earlobe has no cartilage, so it is soft. Many people wear earrings there.

93360.q: What makes the outer ear firm but bendy?
93360.e: There is cartilage in the outer ear. It is firmer than skin, but you can bend it.
93360.m: Cartilage makes the outer ear bendy.

93361.q: Which animal can turn its ears in different directions?
93361.e: Cats have lots of muscles in their ears. They turn their ears towards a sound.
93361.m: A cat can turn its ears.

93362.q: How many ears does a person have?
93362.e: People have one ear on each side of the head. With two ears you can tell better where a sound comes from.
93362.m: With two ears you can hear where a sound comes from.

93363.q: Which animal has especially big ears that it also uses to cool down?
93363.e: African elephants have huge ears. By flapping their ears they cool their blood.
93363.m: Elephants cool down with their ears.

93364.q: Which animals have no outer ears, only hidden ear openings on the head?
93364.e: Birds have no outer ears. Their ear openings are on the sides of the head under the feathers.

93365.q: Can a small hole in the eardrum heal again?
a: Yes, it often heals by itself
Only with a plaster on the outside
Only if you drink lots of milk
93365.e: The eardrum can often close small tears by itself within a few weeks. Even so, a doctor should look at the ear.
93365.m: A small hole in the eardrum often heals by itself.

93366.q: Why is the eardrum called that?
a: It vibrates like the skin of a drum
It is made of animal skin
It is round like a ball
93366.e: A drum has a tight skin stretched over the top. The eardrum is stretched in a similar way and vibrates.
93366.m: The eardrum is stretched like the skin of a drum.

93367.q: What can a very loud bang do to the eardrum?
93367.e: A very strong bang can injure the eardrum. It can get a small hole.
93367.m: A strong bang can injure the eardrum.

93368.q: What are the three tiny bones behind the eardrum called?
93368.e: The three ear bones are named after tools. They pass the vibrations of the eardrum further inside.
93368.m: Behind the eardrum are the hammer, anvil and stirrup.

93369.q: What should you never do right next to another child's ear?
93369.e: A loud shout right next to the ear is very strong. It can hurt and damage the ear.
93369.m: Never shout right into someone's ear.

a: At the end of the ear canal
On the outside of the outer ear
93370.e: The eardrum separates the ear canal from the middle ear. You cannot see it from the outside.
93370.m: The eardrum separates the ear canal from the middle ear.

93371.q: What do you often feel in your ears when a plane is landing?
93371.e: When landing, the air pressure changes. This presses on the eardrum until the pressure evens out again.
93371.m: On a plane your ears often feel pressure.

93372.q: What helps against the pressure in your ears on a plane?
93372.e: When you swallow and chew, a little air flows into the middle ear. That evens out the pressure.
93372.m: Swallowing evens out the pressure in your ears.

93373.q: What is an ear doctor more exactly called?
93373.e: The ears, nose and throat are connected inside. That is why an ear, nose and throat doctor looks after all three.
93373.m: For your ears you go to an ear, nose and throat doctor.

93374.q: What is the yellowish, sticky stuff in the ear canal called?
93374.e: A waxy substance forms in the ear canal. It is called earwax.
93374.m: Earwax forms in the ear canal.

a: It protects the ear from dirt
93375.e: Earwax traps dust and tiny particles. It also keeps the skin in the ear canal soft.

93376.q: Why should you not push cotton buds deep into your ear?
a: They push the earwax further in
93376.e: A cotton bud pushes earwax inwards. It can form a plug or injure the ear.
93376.m: Cotton buds do not belong deep in the ear.

93377.q: How does earwax normally get out of the ear?
a: You have to scrape it out every day
93377.e: The ear cleans itself. The earwax slowly moves to the opening of the ear canal.

93378.q: What is the right way to clean your ears?
a: Poke a pencil into the ear
93378.e: It is enough to clean the outer ear and the entrance of the ear with a flannel. Deep inside the ear needs no cleaning.
93378.m: You only wash the outside part of the ear.

93379.q: What can happen if too much earwax blocks the ear?
93379.e: A plug of earwax can block the ear canal. Then sounds reach the eardrum less well.
93379.m: Too much earwax can muffle your hearing.

93380.q: Who is best at removing a hard plug of earwax?
93380.e: A doctor can remove the plug safely with water or small instruments. That way the ear is not injured.
93380.m: A doctor removes a plug of earwax.

93381.q: What can the doctor put into the ear to make hard earwax soft?
93381.e: Ear drops soften hard earwax. Afterwards it can come out more easily or be rinsed out.
93381.m: Ear drops make hard earwax soft.

93382.e: A jet plane taking off is extremely loud close up. That can damage your ears.
93382.m: A plane taking off is very loud.

93383.e: Rustling leaves are a very quiet sound. The other sounds are much louder.
93383.m: Rustling leaves are a quiet sound.

93384.q: What can music that is too loud in headphones do over time?
93384.e: Very loud sounds can destroy the tiny hearing cells in the inner ear. They do not grow back.
93384.m: Music that is too loud harms your ears.

93385.q: What can you sometimes hear in your ear after a very loud concert?
93385.e: After a lot of noise, your ear sometimes rings or hisses. That is a warning sign that it was too loud.
93385.m: Ringing in the ear warns of too much noise.

93386.q: What is the part of the inner ear that looks like a snail shell called?
93386.e: The cochlea is coiled like a snail shell. Inside it are the hearing cells that report sounds to the brain.
93386.m: The hearing cells sit in the cochlea.

93387.q: Where does a person notice what they hear?
93387.e: The ears pick up the sounds. Only the brain understands what you hear, for example a word or a song.
93387.m: The brain understands what the ears hear.

93388.q: Which symbol is often used for the volume on a mobile phone?
93388.e: A small loudspeaker symbol shows the volume. With the buttons you make it louder or quieter.
93388.m: The loudspeaker symbol stands for the volume.

93389.q: Who often wears ear protection at work?
93389.e: A pneumatic drill is very loud. Ear protection keeps the ears from being damaged.
93389.m: For loud work you wear ear protection.

93390.q: When should children wear ear protection?
93390.e: Fireworks bang very loudly, for example on 1 August. Children's ears are especially sensitive.
93390.m: At fireworks you protect children's ears.

93391.e: Ear protection muffles sound before it reaches the ear. So less noise gets in.

93392.q: During which hobby do many people in Switzerland wear ear protection?
93392.e: A shot is a very loud bang. That is why shooters at the shooting range wear ear protection.
93392.m: When shooting, you protect your ears.

93393.q: What is good for your ears at a loud party if you have no ear protection?
a: Going to a quiet place now and then
Standing right next to the speakers
Turning the music up even louder
93393.e: Breaks in a quiet place let your ears recover. That way they are under less strain.
93393.m: Breaks from noise are good for your ears.

93394.q: Apart from ear protection, what else is good for your ears in a loud place?
93394.e: The further you are from the source of the noise, the quieter it gets. That is why you do not stand right in front of the speakers.
93394.m: Distance from the noise protects your ears.

93395.q: Which animal has no ear protection but hears fireworks especially well and is often frightened?
93395.e: Dogs hear much better than people. That is why the bangs of fireworks often scare them a lot.
93395.m: Dogs are often frightened by fireworks.

93396.q: What does a hearing aid do?
93396.e: A hearing aid picks up sounds and plays them louder into the ear. That way people who are hard of hearing hear better.
93396.m: A hearing aid makes sounds louder.

93397.q: Where do you wear a hearing aid?
93397.e: Many hearing aids sit behind the ear. Others are so small that they fit in the ear canal.
93397.m: You wear a hearing aid on or in the ear.

93398.q: What does a hearing aid need to work?
93398.e: A hearing aid is a small electrical device. It needs power from a battery or a rechargeable battery.
93398.m: A hearing aid runs on power from a battery.

93399.q: Which part of a hearing aid picks up the sounds?
93399.e: A tiny microphone catches the sounds. The device makes them louder and passes them on through a small loudspeaker.
93399.m: A microphone in the hearing aid catches the sounds.

93400.q: Who often needs a hearing aid?
a: People who do not hear well
People who do not see well
93400.e: People who are hard of hearing find it difficult to follow conversations. A hearing aid helps them.
93400.m: People who are hard of hearing often wear a hearing aid.

93401.q: What did people use before there were electric hearing aids?
93401.e: An ear trumpet is a funnel that you hold to your ear. It collects sound and guides it into the ear.
93401.m: In the past, an ear trumpet helped people hear.

93402.q: What should you not do with a hearing aid?
a: Take it out in the evening
93402.e: Most hearing aids are electrical devices and cannot take much water. That is why you take them out to shower.
93402.m: You take the hearing aid out before showering.

93403.q: Which specialist fits a hearing aid?
93403.e: Audiologists test your hearing and set up the hearing aid to suit you. That way you hear well with it.
93403.m: An audiologist sets up the hearing aid.

93404.q: Where in Switzerland do you often hear an echo?
93404.e: If you shout towards a rock face, the shout comes back. That is why there is often an echo in the Alps.
93404.m: In the mountains you often hear an echo.

93405.q: What is needed for an echo to happen?
93405.e: The sound has to bounce off something hard, for example rock. The wall must be far enough away for you to hear the shout separately.
93405.m: An echo needs a hard, distant wall.

93406.q: Which animal finds its way in the dark using echoes?
93406.e: Bats make very high sounds. From the echoes they can tell where obstacles and insects are.
93406.m: Bats find their way using echoes.

93407.q: Why do you hear the echo a little later than your own shout?
a: The sound needs time to travel
The wall only calls back later
93407.e: Sound is fast, but not endlessly fast. It needs time to reach the wall and come back.
93407.m: Sound needs time to travel to the wall.

93408.q: When does an echo come back to you faster?
a: When the rock face is closer
When the rock face is further away
When you shout in a deeper voice
93408.e: The sound has to travel to the wall and back. If the wall is close, the path is short and the echo comes back faster.
93408.m: The closer the wall, the faster the echo comes back.

93409.q: Which sea animal also uses echoes to find its way?
93409.e: Dolphins make clicking sounds. The echoes show them where fish and rocks are.
93409.m: Dolphins find their way with echoes.

93410.q: Where indoors do you often hear sound ringing out like an echo?
a: In a room full of cushions
93410.e: In an empty hall, sound bounces off the hard walls. Soft things would swallow the sound.

93411.q: What do you do when you whisper?
93411.e: When you whisper, you speak without your voice, only with your breath. That is why it is very quiet.

93412.q: Where do people often whisper so as not to disturb others?
93412.e: In a library, people want to read in peace. That is why you speak quietly there.

93413.q: What is the game called where a word is whispered from ear to ear?
93413.e: In Telephone, each child whispers the word into the next child's ear. At the end, something completely different often comes out.

93414.q: What does not vibrate when you whisper, unlike when you speak normally?
93414.e: When you speak normally, the vocal cords in your throat vibrate. When you whisper they stay still, and only the air rushes.
93414.m: When you whisper, the vocal cords do not vibrate.

93415.q: What do you often hold in front of your mouth when you whisper a secret to someone?
93415.e: With your hand next to your mouth, you direct the whisper to the ear. That way the others see and hear less of it.
93415.m: When whispering to someone, you often hold your hand in front of your mouth.

93416.q: Why do you whisper something into someone's ear?
a: So that others do not hear it
So that the ear gets warm
93416.e: A secret is meant for only one person to hear. That is why you whisper it close to the ear.
93416.m: You whisper a secret into someone's ear.

93417.q: When do people often whisper at home?
a: When calling someone from far away
93417.e: A sleeping baby should not wake up. That is why people speak quietly.
93417.m: Next to a sleeping baby, you whisper.

93418.q: What helps if you want to hear someone whispering in a noisy room?
93418.e: Quiet sounds get even quieter with distance. Very close up, you understand a whisper better.
93418.m: You can only understand a whisper from close up.

93419.q: What is a common cause of earache in children?
93419.e: In children, the middle ear often gets inflamed. That hurts and often comes after a cold.
93419.m: A middle ear infection often causes earache.

93420.q: After which illness do children often get earache?
93420.e: With a cold, germs can travel from the nose to the ear. Then the ear gets inflamed.
93420.m: After a cold, the ears often hurt.

93421.q: What should you do if your ear hurts a lot or you also have a fever?
a: Push a cotton bud deep inside
93421.e: Bad earache with a fever should be looked at by a doctor. They can find out what is wrong.
93421.m: With bad earache you go to the doctor.

93422.q: What does the doctor use to look into the ear?
a: A small light with a funnel
93422.e: The instrument is called an otoscope. It has a light and a small funnel so you can see as far as the eardrum.
93422.m: You look into the ear with an otoscope.

93423.q: What can often cause earache after swimming?
a: Water that stays in the ear canal
93423.e: If water stays in the ear canal for a long time, the skin gets soft. Then germs can cause an infection.
93423.m: Water in the ear can lead to an infection.

93424.q: What protects your ears in a cold wind?
93424.e: A cold wind can make your ears hurt. A hat or a headband keeps your ears warm.
93424.m: A hat protects your ears from the cold.

93425.q: What do you do if your ear hurts?
a: Pour cold water into your ear
93425.e: Sharp things can injure the ear canal or the eardrum. If it hurts, leave your ear alone and tell a grown-up who will take you to the doctor.
93425.m: Sharp objects never belong in the ear.

93426.q: What helps if your ears feel pressure when travelling up a mountain?
a: Holding your breath for a long time
93426.e: A thin tube connects the ear with the throat. When you swallow or yawn it opens, the air pressure evens out and the pressure stops.
93426.m: Swallowing helps when your ears feel pressure.

93427.q: What do you use to speak in sign language?
93427.e: In sign language you show words with your hands, face and body. You see the language instead of hearing it.
93427.m: Sign language is spoken with the hands and face.

93428.e: Deaf people cannot hear spoken language. With sign language they can talk with each other easily.
93428.m: Deaf people often use sign language.

93429.q: How many sign languages are there in Switzerland?
93429.e: In Switzerland there is a Swiss German, a French and an Italian sign language. They belong to the language regions.
93429.m: There are three sign languages in Switzerland.

93430.q: Is there only one sign language in the whole world?
93430.e: Just like spoken languages, there are many different sign languages. Each country usually has its own.
93430.m: There are many different sign languages.

93431.q: How do you spell out a name in sign language?
93431.e: In the finger alphabet, each letter has its own hand sign. That way you can spell out names.
93431.m: Names are spelled out with the finger alphabet.

93432.q: Why is the face important in sign language?
93432.e: With your face you show whether you are asking something or whether you are happy or angry. It is part of the grammar.
93432.m: The face is part of sign language.

93433.q: How do deaf people often applaud?
a: They wave both hands in the air
93433.e: You cannot see clapping, only hear it. That is why deaf people wave their raised hands, which everyone can see.
93433.m: Deaf people applaud with waving hands.

93434.q: Who translates between spoken language and sign language?
93434.e: Sign language interpreters translate on television, for example. You then see them in a small picture at the edge of the screen.

a: You cannot hear, or can hardly hear
93435.e: Deaf people hear nothing or almost nothing. Some are deaf from birth, others become deaf later.
93435.m: Deaf people hear nothing or almost nothing.

93436.q: How does a deaf person know that someone is ringing the doorbell?
93436.e: For many deaf people, the doorbell is connected to a lamp. Instead of a sound, a light flashes.
93436.m: Deaf people see the doorbell as a light signal.

93437.q: Which famous composer went deaf during his life?
93437.e: Ludwig van Beethoven gradually lost his hearing. Even so, he went on writing great music.
93437.m: Beethoven composed even though he went deaf.

93438.q: What helps deaf people understand a film?
93438.e: Subtitles show what is said as text at the bottom of the picture. That way you can read along.

93439.q: Which device is placed in the ear of some deaf people during an operation?
93439.e: A cochlear implant sends sounds as electrical signals straight to the hearing nerve. That way some deaf people can perceive sounds again.
93439.m: A cochlear implant can help with hearing.

93440.q: What is it called when you recognise words from someone's lips?
93440.e: Some deaf people watch the mouth closely. From the movements of the lips they recognise some of the words.
93440.m: In lip reading you recognise words from the mouth.

93441.q: What is important when you talk to a person who lip-reads?
a: Look at them and speak clearly
Cover your mouth with your hand
93441.e: The person must be able to see your mouth well. Speaking clearly while looking at them helps them understand.
93441.m: Speaking clearly and looking at the person helps with lip reading.

93442.q: What can deaf people still feel, for example at a concert?
93442.e: Deep notes make the floor and the body vibrate. Deaf people can feel music this way.
93442.m: You can also feel music as vibration.

93443.q: Why do people put earplugs in their ears?
93443.e: Earplugs block the ear canal. So less noise gets into the ear.

93444.q: What are many earplugs for sleeping made of?
93444.e: You squeeze foam earplugs and put them in your ear. There they expand and seal well.
93444.m: Many earplugs are made of foam.

93445.q: When do earplugs help you sleep?
a: When someone in the room snores
93445.e: Snoring can disturb your sleep. Earplugs make the noise quieter.
93445.m: Earplugs help against disturbing noises while you sleep.

93446.q: Why do some children wear earplugs when swimming?
a: So that no water gets into the ear
So that they can see under water
So that they do not get cold
93446.e: Special earplugs keep the water out. That is important if someone often gets ear infections.
93446.m: Swimming earplugs keep water out of the ear.

93447.q: What were many earplugs made of in the past?
93447.e: Soft wax can be shaped and seals the ear canal well. Earplugs like this still exist today.
93447.m: Wax earplugs have been around for a long time.

93448.q: What should you do with used foam earplugs?
a: Replace them with new ones soon
Leave them in your ear all day
93448.e: Foam earplugs get dirty over time. That is why you replace them regularly, so the ear stays clean.
93448.m: You soon replace used foam earplugs.

93449.q: How do you put foam earplugs in properly?
a: Roll them up and put them in the ear
Squash them flat and lay them on the ear
Wet them and push them in
Press them deep in with a pencil
93449.e: You roll the earplug thin and put it into the ear canal. There it gets thicker again and seals.
93449.m: You roll up foam earplugs before putting them in.

93450.q: In an ancient Greek legend, whose men blocked their ears so as not to hear the song of the Sirens?
93450.e: The sailors of Odysseus blocked their ears. So they did not hear the dangerous song and sailed safely past.
93450.m: Odysseus's men blocked their ears against the Sirens.

93451.q: Where does the echo get its name from?
a: From a nymph in a Greek legend
93451.e: In a Greek legend, the nymph Echo could only repeat the last words of others. The echo is named after her.
93451.m: The echo is named after a nymph.

93452.q: What can you do with your hands so that a shout can be heard further away?
a: Hold them like a funnel at your mouth
93452.e: Hands held like a funnel send the sound in one direction. That way the shout carries further.
93452.m: Cupping your hands round your mouth makes a shout carry further.

93453.q: Which mirror in a car helps the driver see behind?
93453.e: In the rear-view mirror, the driver sees what is happening behind the car without turning round.
93453.m: The rear-view mirror lets you see behind.

93454.q: What is an ordinary bathroom mirror made of?
93454.e: A mirror is a pane of glass. At the back there is a thin layer of metal such as silver or aluminium.
93454.m: Behind the glass of a mirror there is a thin layer of metal.

93455.e: Only a very smooth, shiny surface reflects light properly. Rough surfaces scatter light in all directions.
93455.m: Smooth and shiny surfaces reflect well.

93456.q: What in nature can act like a mirror?
93456.e: When a lake is completely calm, its surface is smooth. Then you can see mountains and trees reflected in it.
93456.m: Calm water can act like a mirror.

93457.q: What do you see in a mirror in a completely dark room?
93457.e: A mirror needs light that it can reflect. Without light you can't see anything in the mirror.

93458.q: How is a beam of light reflected when it hits a mirror at an angle?
a: At an angle to the other side
93458.e: Light bounces off a mirror like a ball off a wall. If it comes in at an angle from the left, it leaves at an angle to the right.
93458.m: Light hitting a mirror at an angle bounces off at an angle to the other side.

93459.q: What appears on the wall when you direct sunlight there with a small mirror?
93459.e: The mirror throws the sunlight onto the wall. There you see a bright spot that you can move around.
93459.m: You can direct sunlight with a mirror.

93460.q: What were mirrors made of a very long time ago, before there were glass mirrors?
93460.e: Long ago, people polished metal such as bronze until it shone. They could see their reflection in it.
93460.m: Long ago, people saw their reflection in shiny polished metal.

93461.q: Why is there a large round mirror at some exits where it is hard to see?
93461.e: Traffic mirrors like these show whether a car or bike is coming from the side. That way you can see round the corner.
93461.m: A traffic mirror helps you see round the corner.

93462.q: You raise your right hand in front of the mirror. Which hand does your reflection seem to raise?
93462.e: In a mirror, right and left seem to be swapped. Your reflection looks as if it is raising its left hand.
93462.m: In a mirror, right and left seem to be swapped.

93463.q: You are standing 1 metre in front of a mirror. How far behind the mirror does your reflection seem to be?
93463.e: Your reflection seems to be exactly as far behind the mirror as you are in front of it.
93463.m: Your reflection is as far behind the mirror as you are in front of it.

93464.q: What does your reflection do when you walk closer to the mirror?
93464.e: Your reflection is always as far behind the mirror as you are in front of it. If you move closer, it comes towards you too.

93465.q: How big is your reflection in a flat mirror?
93465.e: A flat mirror shows everything at the right size. Only curved mirrors make it bigger or smaller.
93465.m: A flat mirror shows you at the same size.

93466.q: Which way up is your reflection in a flat wall mirror?
93466.e: In a flat mirror the picture is upright. The head is at the top, the feet are at the bottom.
93466.m: In a flat mirror the reflection is upright.

a: No, it is only a picture
93467.e: Your reflection seems to be behind the mirror. But there is nothing there; it is only a picture made of light.

93468.q: Which animal can recognise itself in a mirror?
93468.e: Chimpanzees realise that they are seeing themselves in the mirror. Researchers showed this with the mirror test.
93468.m: Chimpanzees recognise themselves in a mirror.

93469.q: At about what age do small children usually recognise themselves in a mirror?
93469.e: At first, babies think their reflection is another child. At about one and a half, they realise it is themselves.
93469.m: Toddlers recognise themselves in a mirror at about one and a half.

93470.q: How big does a wall mirror need to be, at least, for you to see yourself from head to toe?
93470.e: Surprising but true: a mirror half as tall as you is enough. It just has to be hung correctly.
93470.m: A mirror half your height is enough to see all of yourself.

93471.q: What is the easiest way to read mirror writing?
93471.e: If you hold mirror writing up to a mirror, it gets turned round again. Then you can read it normally.
93471.m: Mirror writing is best read with a mirror.

93472.q: Which famous artist wrote many notes in mirror writing?
93472.e: Leonardo da Vinci lived in Italy over 500 years ago. In his notebooks he often wrote from right to left in mirror writing.
93472.m: Leonardo da Vinci often wrote in mirror writing.

93473.q: Which capital letter looks exactly the same in a mirror?
93473.e: The letter A is built the same on the left and right. That is why it looks the same in a mirror as before.
93473.m: An A looks the same in a mirror.

93474.q: Which name in capital letters looks exactly the same in mirror writing?
93474.e: The letters O and T are the same on the left and right. And OTTO is the same forwards and backwards.
93474.m: The name OTTO looks the same in a mirror.

93475.q: Which letter is often mixed up with “b” when learning to write, because it looks like its mirror image?
93475.e: The b has its belly on the right, the d on the left. In a mirror, a b turns into a d.
93475.m: In a mirror, a b becomes a d.

93476.q: Which digit looks exactly the same in a mirror?
93476.e: The 8 is built the same on the left and right. The other digits look back to front in a mirror.
93476.m: The digit 8 looks the same in a mirror.

93477.q: What does a funhouse mirror do to your reflection?
93477.e: A funhouse mirror shows you, for example, very fat, very thin or stretched out. That looks funny.
93477.m: A funhouse mirror distorts your reflection.

93478.q: What is the surface of a funhouse mirror like?
93478.e: A funhouse mirror is not flat but bent. This curve distorts the picture.

93479.q: You look very fat in a funhouse mirror. What has really happened?
93479.e: You stay the same; only the curved mirror distorts the light. That is why the picture looks different.
93479.m: In a funhouse mirror only the picture changes, not you.

93480.q: Which shiny Christmas decoration distorts your reflection like a funhouse mirror?
93480.e: A shiny Christmas bauble is round and curved. In it you see yourself distorted and small.
93480.m: A shiny bauble works like a funhouse mirror.

93481.q: Why can a funhouse mirror show you thin at the top and fat at the bottom?
a: It is curved differently at the top and bottom
It is dirty at the top
It is colder at the top
93481.e: A funhouse mirror is bent differently in different places. Each place distorts the picture in a different way.
93481.m: Different curves distort the picture differently.

93482.q: What do you look like in crumpled kitchen foil?
a: You can't see yourself at all
93482.e: Kitchen foil is shiny, but when crumpled it is full of creases. That is why your picture becomes distorted and blurred.
93482.m: Crumpled foil only shows a distorted picture.

93483.q: What is a room at a funfair with lots of funhouse mirrors called?
93483.e: In a hall of mirrors there are lots of funhouse mirrors. You laugh because you look so funny.
93483.m: A hall of mirrors has lots of funhouse mirrors.

93484.q: What is a rear-view mirror in a car for?
93484.e: With the rear-view mirror, the driver sees what is behind the car. He doesn't have to turn round to do this.
93484.m: The rear-view mirror lets you see behind.

93485.q: Where is the inside mirror in a car?
a: At the top in the middle of the windscreen
93485.e: The inside mirror hangs at the top in the middle of the front windscreen. In it, the driver can see behind through the rear window.
93485.m: The inside mirror hangs at the top of the windscreen.

93486.q: How many wing mirrors does an ordinary car usually have?
93486.e: A car has one wing mirror on the left and one on the right. There is usually also the inside mirror.
93486.m: A car usually has two wing mirrors.

93487.q: What is the area next to a vehicle that the driver can't see in the mirrors called?
93487.e: Even with mirrors, there are places the driver can't see. This area is called the blind spot.
93487.m: In the blind spot, the driver can't see anything.

93488.q: As a cyclist next to a lorry, what should you always keep in mind?
a: The driver may not see you
93488.e: Lorries have a large blind spot. It is better to stay behind the lorry and make eye contact with the driver.
93488.m: Next to a lorry, you can easily be overlooked.

93489.q: Where do you fit a mirror on a bike?
93489.e: A bike mirror is usually fitted on the handlebars or on the helmet. That way you can see cars coming from behind.
93489.m: On a bike, the mirror is usually on the handlebars.

93490.q: Why are some wing mirrors slightly curved?
a: So that you can see more
So that they shine more nicely
93490.e: A curved mirror shows a larger area. But things in it look a little smaller.
93490.m: A curved wing mirror shows more of the road.

93491.q: Why can you dip the inside mirror of a car at night?
a: So that headlights behind don't dazzle you
So that it gets warmer in the car
So that the car goes faster
So that the mirror stays clean
93491.e: At night, the headlights of cars behind shine straight into the mirror. When it is dipped, the driver is no longer dazzled.
93491.m: At night you dip the inside mirror.

93492.q: What do you use a magnifying glass for?
93492.e: Through a magnifying glass, small things look much bigger. That way you can make out fine details.
93492.m: A magnifying glass makes small things look bigger.

93493.q: What shape is the lens of a magnifying glass?
93493.e: A magnifying lens curves outwards. It is thicker in the middle than at the edge.
93493.m: A magnifying lens is thicker in the middle than at the edge.

93494.q: Which famous detective is often shown with a magnifying glass?
93494.e: Sherlock Holmes is a made-up detective. In pictures he often searches for clues with a magnifying glass.
93494.m: Sherlock Holmes searches for clues with a magnifying glass.

93495.q: Why shouldn't you leave a magnifying glass lying in the sun?
93495.e: A magnifying glass gathers sunlight into a small, hot spot. Paper or dry grass can start to burn there.
93495.m: A magnifying glass in the sun can start a fire.

93496.q: What must you never do with a magnifying glass?
93496.e: The magnifying glass strongly focuses sunlight. That can seriously injure your eyes.
93496.m: Never look at the sun through a magnifying glass.

93497.q: What can act like a tiny magnifying glass?
93497.e: A drop of water is round and curved like a lens. On a leaf it makes the veins look bigger.
93497.m: A drop of water can act like a magnifying glass.

93498.q: What do you use a bug viewer (a magnifying pot) for?
93498.e: In a bug viewer you can keep a beetle or an ant for a short time. Through the lid you see the animal magnified.
93498.m: In a bug viewer you look at small animals.

93499.q: What can you see well on your fingertip with a magnifying glass?
93499.e: Everyone has fine lines on their fingertips. These ridges make the fingerprint.
93499.m: With a magnifying glass you can see the ridges of your fingerprint.

93500.q: Why do many people wear glasses?
93500.e: If the eyes don't see sharply, glasses help. Their lenses guide the light into the eye correctly.

93501.q: Where do you usually get new glasses?
93501.e: The optician measures your eyes and fits the glasses. For eye problems, the eye doctor can help too.
93501.m: You get glasses at the optician's.

93502.q: What do sunglasses protect your eyes from?
93502.e: Good sunglasses block glaring light and harmful UV rays. That protects the eyes.
93502.m: Sunglasses protect your eyes from glaring light.

93503.q: What does a short-sighted person see blurrily without glasses?
93503.e: Short-sighted people see close things sharply. What is far away, like the board at school, they see blurrily.
93503.m: Short-sighted people see blurrily in the distance.

93504.q: What can you put directly on your eye instead of wearing glasses?
93504.e: Contact lenses are small, thin shells. They sit directly on the eye and work like the lenses in glasses.

93505.q: What do many older people need reading glasses for?
a: To read small print close up
93505.e: As people get older, their eyes find it harder to focus on close things. Reading glasses help with reading.
93505.m: Older people often need reading glasses.

93506.q: Which glasses protect you from snow and wind when skiing?
93506.e: Ski goggles fit closely around the eyes. They protect from wind, snow and glaring light.
93506.m: When skiing, ski goggles protect your eyes.

93507.q: In which country were the first glasses made over 700 years ago?
93507.e: The first glasses appeared around 1300 in northern Italy. They didn't have arms yet and just sat on the nose.
93507.m: The first glasses came from Italy.

93508.q: What are the parts of a pair of glasses that rest over the ears called?
93508.e: The arms hold the glasses in place behind the ears. The bridge rests on the nose.
93508.m: The arms of glasses rest over the ears.

93510.q: In which vehicle do people use a periscope to look above the water?
93510.e: A submarine dives under water. With the periscope, the crew looks above the surface of the water.
93510.m: In a submarine you look up out of the water with the periscope.

93511.q: How many mirrors does a simple periscope need?
93511.e: At the top, one mirror directs the light down into the tube. At the bottom, a second mirror directs it into the eye.
93511.m: A simple periscope has two mirrors.

93512.q: What can you use a periscope for on land?
93512.e: With a periscope you can see over obstacles without climbing over them yourself.
93512.m: With a periscope you can see over a wall.

93513.q: How are the two mirrors placed in a simple periscope?
93513.e: Both mirrors are fitted at an angle. That way they direct the light round the corner into the tube and out again.
93513.m: The mirrors in a periscope are fitted at an angle.

93514.q: What can you use to make a simple periscope yourself?
93514.e: You can take an empty milk carton, for example. At the top and bottom you glue in a small mirror at an angle.
93514.m: You can make a periscope from cardboard and two mirrors.

93515.q: Which way up is the picture in a simple periscope with two mirrors?
93515.e: The first mirror turns the picture, the second turns it back. So you see everything upright.
93515.m: In a periscope you see the picture upright.

93516.q: What does the word “periscope” roughly mean?
93516.e: The word comes from Greek. “Peri” means around and “skopein” means to look.

93517.q: What do you see when you look into a kaleidoscope?
93517.e: In a kaleidoscope, colourful, regular patterns appear. They often look like a star.
93517.m: In a kaleidoscope you see colourful patterns.

93518.e: Strips of mirror are fitted inside the tube. At the end there are colourful pieces of glass or beads.
93518.m: A kaleidoscope contains mirrors and colourful pieces.

93519.q: What happens when you turn a kaleidoscope?
93519.e: When you turn it, the colourful pieces tumble about. The mirrors immediately make a new pattern from them.
93519.m: Turning a kaleidoscope makes a new pattern.

93520.q: What are the patterns in a kaleidoscope like?
a: All jumbled up with no order
93520.e: The mirrors repeat the colourful pieces several times. That is why the patterns are regular, like a star or a flower.
93520.m: The mirrors make regular patterns in a kaleidoscope.

93521.q: About how many years ago was the kaleidoscope invented?
93521.e: The Scotsman David Brewster invented the kaleidoscope in 1816. That is about 200 years ago.
93521.m: The kaleidoscope was invented about 200 years ago.

93522.q: What does the word “kaleidoscope” roughly mean?
93522.e: The word comes from Greek. It roughly means “seeing beautiful shapes”.

93523.q: How often do you see exactly the same pattern again in a kaleidoscope?
93523.e: The pieces fall differently by chance every time. That is why exactly the same pattern almost never appears twice.
93523.m: In a kaleidoscope, a pattern almost never repeats.

93524.q: Where is it best to point a kaleidoscope when you look into it?
93524.e: The colourful pieces only light up when light shines through them. That is why you hold the kaleidoscope up to a window or a lamp.
93524.m: You hold a kaleidoscope up to the light.

93525.e: In a mirror maze there are very many mirrors. You often have to search for the way through.
93525.m: A mirror maze is a room full of mirrors.

93526.q: Where in Switzerland do you often find a mirror maze?
93526.e: At the Chilbi, the funfair, there are often mirror mazes. You can get lost there between the mirrors.
93526.m: At the Chilbi there is often a mirror maze.

93527.q: In which Swiss city is there a famous mirror maze in the Glacier Garden?
93527.e: In the Glacier Garden in Lucerne there is the mirror maze “Alhambra”. It is over 100 years old.
93527.m: In the Glacier Garden in Lucerne there is a mirror maze.

93528.q: Why is it easy to get lost in a mirror maze?
a: You don't know what is real
93528.e: The mirrors show lots of passages that don't really exist. You don't know where a real path is.
93528.m: In a mirror maze you see lots of false passages.

93529.q: What do you see if you stand between two mirrors hanging exactly opposite each other?
a: Lots of reflections one behind the other
93529.e: The mirrors reflect each other again and again. That makes a long row of reflections.
93529.m: Two mirrors facing each other show lots of reflections.

93530.q: What helps you not to walk into a mirror in a mirror maze?
a: Stretching your hands out in front
93530.e: With your hands stretched out, you feel the mirror before you bump into it with your head.
93530.m: In a mirror maze you stretch your hands out in front.

93531.q: In which famous palace in France is there a large Hall of Mirrors?
93531.e: In the Palace of Versailles near Paris there is the Hall of Mirrors. Hundreds of mirrors hang on its walls.
93531.m: The Palace of Versailles has a famous Hall of Mirrors.

93532.q: How does your reflection look on the inside of a shiny spoon?
93532.e: The inside of the spoon curves inwards. If you look into it from a little further away, your picture is upside down.
93532.m: In the bowl of a spoon you are upside down.

93533.q: How do you look on the back of a shiny spoon?
93533.e: The back of the spoon curves outwards. In it, your picture is upright but smaller.
93533.m: On the back of a spoon you are upright and small.

93534.q: What do you call a mirror that curves inwards like the inside of a spoon?
93534.e: A mirror that curves inwards is called a concave mirror. The bowl of a spoon is a small concave mirror.
93534.m: The inside of a spoon is a concave mirror.

93535.q: What do you call a mirror that curves outwards like the back of a spoon?
93535.e: A mirror that curves outwards is called a convex mirror. It shows everything smaller, but a large area.
93535.m: The back of a spoon is a convex mirror.

93536.q: Why is your reflection in a spoon distorted?
a: Because the spoon is made of wood
93536.e: A spoon is not flat but bent. Bent mirrors distort the picture.
93536.m: A spoon distorts the picture because it is curved.

93537.e: A metal spoon that is polished smooth and shiny reflects light well. Wood and scratches scatter the light.
93537.m: A shiny metal spoon reflects well.

93538.q: How is the Olympic flame lit at Olympia in Greece?
a: With sunlight and a concave mirror
With an oil lamp from a temple
93538.e: At Olympia, a concave mirror focuses sunlight on one point. It gets so hot there that the torch catches fire.
93538.m: The Olympic flame is lit with a concave mirror.

93539.q: What is behind the bulb of a torch so that the light shines forwards?
93539.e: Behind the bulb there is a shiny concave mirror. It collects the light and sends it forwards.
93539.m: A concave mirror directs a torch's light forwards.

93540.q: Which instrument lets you look at tiny things like cells very greatly magnified?
93540.e: A microscope magnifies much more strongly than a magnifying glass. With it you can even see tiny cells.

93541.q: What lets you see faraway animals in the forest closer?
93541.e: Binoculars seem to bring faraway things closer.
93541.m: With binoculars you see faraway things closer.

93542.q: A magnifying glass magnifies 3 times. How long does a 2 cm beetle look through it?
93542.e: 3 times means three times as big. So 2 cm times 3 equals 6 cm.
93542.m: With 3 times magnification, everything looks three times as big.

93543.e: With 10 times magnification, a thing looks ten times as big as it really is.
93543.m: 10 times means ten times as big.

93544.q: What do stargazers use to look at the Moon magnified?
93544.e: A telescope is a large instrument for looking at faraway things. With it you can see craters on the Moon and distant planets.
93544.m: With a telescope you see the Moon magnified.

93545.q: Which mirror in the bathroom shows your face magnified?
93545.e: A make-up mirror curves slightly inwards. If you look into it close up, your face looks bigger.
93545.m: A make-up mirror magnifies your face.

93546.q: Does an ant really get bigger when you look at it through a magnifying glass?
a: Yes, when the sun is shining
93546.e: The magnifying glass only bends the light differently. The ant itself stays exactly the same size.
93546.m: A magnifying glass doesn't really make things bigger.

93547.q: A pencil is 1 cm thick and looks 4 cm thick through a magnifying glass. How many times does the glass magnify?
93547.e: 1 cm becomes 4 cm. 4 divided by 1 is 4, so the glass magnifies 4 times.
93547.m: The magnification tells you how many times bigger something looks.

93548.q: What happens to your picture in the bowl of a spoon when you get very close?
a: It is upright and becomes big
It stays upside down and tiny
93548.e: Very close to a concave mirror, the picture turns round. It is then upright and magnified.
93548.m: Very close to the spoon, you see yourself upright and big.

93549.q: What does your reflection look like on a soap bubble?
93549.e: A soap bubble is round and shiny. Like a funhouse mirror, it shows you small and distorted.
93549.m: A soap bubble shows you small and distorted.

93550.q: Which country built the GPS satellite navigation system and operates it?
93550.e: GPS was developed by the US Department of Defense. Today it is operated by the US Space Force and used all over the world.
93550.m: GPS is a navigation system of the USA.

93551.q: From at least how many satellites does a GPS receiver need signals to work out its position and altitude accurately?
93551.e: Three satellites would be enough for the position if the clock in the receiver were perfect. The fourth satellite makes up for the error of the receiver’s clock.
93551.m: For an accurate position, GPS needs at least four satellites.

93552.q: Why are China and Europe building their own navigation systems, even though GPS exists?
a: They do not want to depend on the USA
GPS does not work outside the USA
Their mobile phones do not understand GPS
93552.e: GPS belongs to the USA, which could restrict it in an emergency. That is why China has built its own system, BeiDou, and Europe has built Galileo.
93552.m: Their own navigation systems make countries independent of GPS.

93553.q: Which device on board GPS satellites is especially important for working out positions?
93553.e: The receiver calculates the distance to each satellite from the travel time of the signals. This needs extremely accurate atomic clocks.
93553.m: Atomic clocks make GPS positioning accurate.

93554.q: What is the name of the European satellite navigation system that Switzerland also takes part in?
93554.e: Galileo is the navigation system of the European Union. Switzerland takes part in it through an agreement with the EU.
93554.m: Galileo is the European counterpart to GPS.

93555.q: What does a GPS receiver actually measure to calculate its distance from a satellite?
a: The travel time of the radio signal
93555.e: Radio signals travel at the speed of light. The distance follows from the time the signal takes.
93555.m: GPS calculates distances from the travel time of radio signals.

93556.q: What can a device with GPS work out?
93556.e: A GPS receiver uses the signals from several satellites to calculate where it is. The system has been fully working since 1995.
93556.m: With GPS you work out your location.

93557.q: What do the pictures from weather satellites mainly show?
a: Clouds and weather systems from above
The roads with all the cars
93557.e: Weather satellites photograph the Earth from above. Their pictures show where clouds, fronts and storms are.
93557.m: Weather satellites show the clouds from above.

93558.q: What are the European weather satellites called whose pictures MeteoSwiss also uses?
93558.e: Meteosat satellites are operated by the organisation EUMETSAT. Switzerland is a member and uses the data for weather forecasts.
93558.m: MeteoSwiss uses pictures from the Meteosat satellites.

93559.q: At what height above the equator are geostationary weather satellites like Meteosat?
93559.e: At about 36,000 km, one orbit takes exactly as long as one turn of the Earth. The satellite then seems to stand still above one point.
93559.m: Geostationary satellites are at a height of about 36,000 km.

93560.q: Why can weather satellites take pictures of clouds at night too?
93560.e: Clouds, land and sea give off heat radiation. Infrared cameras measure this radiation even without sunlight.
93560.m: With infrared, weather satellites can see clouds at night too.

93561.q: What advantage do weather satellites in a polar orbit have?
a: Bit by bit they fly over the whole Earth
They fly more than 1 million km away
93561.e: Polar satellites orbit over the poles at a height of about 800 km. Because the Earth turns beneath them, they see the whole Earth over time.
93561.m: Satellites in polar orbits observe the whole Earth.

93562.q: Which dangerous weather events over the sea can be spotted early thanks to weather satellites?
93562.e: Tropical storms form over warm seas, where there are hardly any measuring stations. Satellite pictures show their cloud spirals early.

93563.q: Which organisation based in Darmstadt operates the European weather satellites?
93563.e: EUMETSAT is the European organisation for weather satellites. Switzerland is one of its member states.
93563.m: EUMETSAT operates the European weather satellites.

93564.q: Why do geostationary weather satellites only see the polar regions badly?
93564.e: Geostationary satellites are high above the equator. They only see the polar regions at a very steep slant at the edge of the picture.
93564.m: From above the equator, a satellite sees the poles only badly.

93566.q: Roughly how long does a signal take from the Earth to a geostationary satellite 36,000 km up and back?
93566.e: Radio travels at about 300,000 km per second. 72,000 km divided by 300,000 km/s makes about 0.24 seconds.
93566.m: Signals via geostationary satellites have a short delay.

93567.q: What are communication satellites needed for?
a: To send TV, phone calls and internet over long distances
To make stars shine more brightly
To keep aeroplanes in the air
93567.e: Communication satellites receive signals from the Earth and send them back to a place far away. This is how TV pictures even get across oceans.
93567.m: Communication satellites pass signals on around the Earth.

93568.q: Where is a geostationary satellite, seen from the Earth?
a: It circles the Earth once an hour
It flies to the Moon every day
It is always above the North Pole
93568.e: A geostationary satellite circles the Earth exactly as fast as the Earth turns. That is why it seems to stand still above the equator, and satellite dishes can point at it all the time.
93568.m: A geostationary satellite seems to stand still above the Earth.

93569.q: What is the smallest number of geostationary satellites needed to cover almost the whole Earth except the poles?
93569.e: Each geostationary satellite sees about a third of the Earth. Three satellites evenly spaced are enough for almost the whole Earth.
93569.m: Three geostationary satellites cover almost the whole Earth.

93570.q: Why do you often need a satellite phone on a ship in the middle of the ocean?
a: There are no mobile phone masts there
It is cheaper than a letter
Mobile phones are banned on ships
93570.e: Mobile phone masts are only on land. A satellite phone sends its signal straight to a satellite and works almost everywhere.
93570.m: Satellite phones also work far away from mobile phone masts.

93571.q: How does a TV signal get from one continent to another by satellite?
a: It goes from the Earth to the satellite and back again
It runs through a cable to the satellite
It jumps from cloud to cloud
It is passed on by the Moon
93571.e: A transmitting antenna sends the signal up to the satellite. The satellite sends it back down to receiving antennas far away on the Earth.
93571.m: Satellites pass signals on from the Earth back to the Earth.

93572.q: What is the curved part called that catches and focuses the weak signals from a TV satellite?
93572.e: The satellite dish, a parabolic antenna, reflects the signals onto one point, like a concave mirror. The receiver sits there.
93572.m: A satellite dish focuses satellite signals.

93573.q: What is meant by space junk?
a: Old satellites and debris in space
93573.e: Space junk is human-made parts that circle the Earth uselessly. It includes old satellites, rocket stages and fragments.
93573.m: Space junk is useless rubbish in orbit around the Earth.

93574.q: Roughly how fast do pieces of junk in low Earth orbit travel?
93574.e: In low orbit, everything has to travel at about 7.8 km per second. That is about 28,000 km/h.
93574.m: Space junk travels faster than a bullet.

93575.q: According to ESA, roughly how many pieces of junk larger than 10 cm circle the Earth (as of the end of 2024)?
93575.e: According to ESA’s 2025 report, over 50,000 pieces larger than 10 cm were circling the Earth at the end of 2024. There are many more smaller pieces.
93575.m: Tens of thousands of large pieces of junk circle the Earth.

93576.q: Why is it dangerous when pieces of junk collide in space?
a: They all fall onto cities at once
93576.e: In every collision the parts break into many smaller pieces of debris. These can hit other satellites, and so there is more and more junk.
93576.m: Collisions in space create more and more junk.

93577.q: What can be done so that there is less new space junk?
a: Let old satellites burn up on purpose
93577.e: Many new satellites are meant to be lowered at the end of their work so that they burn up in the atmosphere. That way they do not stay in orbit as junk.
93577.m: Old satellites should burn up at the end instead of circling as junk.

93578.q: What does the International Space Station ISS do when a piece of junk comes too close?
a: It moves out of the way using its engines
It catches it in a net
93578.e: Ground stations calculate the path of the debris. If the risk is too high, the ISS raises or lowers its orbit a little.
93578.m: The ISS moves out of the way of dangerous junk.

93579.q: What happens to many pieces of junk in low orbit after a while?
a: They burn up in the atmosphere
They land gently in the sea
93579.e: The thin air slowly slows the parts down. They sink and burn up as they enter the atmosphere.
93579.m: Junk flying low burns up in the atmosphere at some point.

93580.q: Which country destroyed one of its own weather satellites with a missile in 2007, creating a lot of space junk?
93580.e: In 2007 China shot down its old weather satellite Fengyun-1C. This produced more than 3,000 recorded pieces of debris.
93580.m: A missile test in 2007 created a large cloud of debris.

93581.q: Which company runs the Starlink satellite internet?
93581.e: Starlink belongs to the American space company SpaceX. It launches the satellites with its own rockets.
93581.m: Starlink is a satellite network run by SpaceX.

93582.q: At roughly what height do most Starlink satellites orbit?
93582.e: Starlink satellites fly in low orbit at about 550 km. That is why the signals are faster than via geostationary satellites.
93582.m: Starlink satellites fly at a low height.

93583.q: Roughly how many Starlink satellites were in space in 2026?
93583.e: Since 2019 SpaceX has kept launching new Starlink satellites. In March 2026 there were over 10,000 in space at the same time for the first time.
93583.m: Starlink is the largest satellite network in the world.

93584.q: In which year was the first group of 60 Starlink satellites launched?
93584.e: On 24 May 2019 a Falcon 9 rocket took the first 60 working Starlink satellites into space.
93584.m: The first Starlink satellites were launched in 2019.

93585.q: Why do many astronomers complain about Starlink?
a: The satellites leave streaks of light on pictures of the sky
The satellites block out the Sun
The satellites change the constellations for ever
93585.e: The satellites reflect sunlight. On long-exposure photos they draw bright lines across the pictures.
93585.m: Large numbers of satellites disturb observation of the night sky.

93586.q: How do newer Starlink satellites exchange data with each other?
93586.e: Newer Starlink satellites have laser links. This lets them pass data on in space, even over the sea.
93586.m: Starlink satellites connect to each other with laser beams.

93587.q: Why is internet via Starlink faster than via geostationary satellites?
a: The satellites are much closer to the Earth
93587.e: Starlink flies at about 550 km instead of 36,000 km. The signals have a much shorter path.
93587.m: The closer the satellite, the shorter the delay.

93588.q: What can you sometimes see in the evening sky shortly after a Starlink launch?
a: A chain of bright points of light
93588.e: Newly launched Starlink satellites fly close behind one another. They then look like a glowing string of pearls.
93588.m: New Starlink satellites look like a string of lights.

93589.q: Which Swiss university leads the scientific side of the CHEOPS space mission?
93589.e: The University of Bern leads a consortium from eleven countries. The mission is a joint project with ESA, and the University of Geneva also plays an important part.
93589.m: CHEOPS is led by the University of Bern.

93590.q: What does the CHEOPS space telescope study?
93590.e: CHEOPS measures known planets around other stars very precisely. This tells researchers more about their size.

93591.q: When was CHEOPS launched into space?
93591.e: CHEOPS was launched on 18 December 2019 on a Soyuz rocket from the European spaceport in French Guiana.

93592.q: How does CHEOPS detect a planet in front of its star?
a: The star becomes slightly dimmer for a short time
93592.e: When a planet passes in front of its star, it blocks a little light. This method is called the transit method.
93592.m: A planet in front of its star makes the star briefly dimmer.

93593.q: What flew into space on two titanium plates on board CHEOPS?
a: A Swiss flag made of cloth
93593.e: Children could send in drawings for CHEOPS. 2,748 of them were chosen by lottery and engraved, greatly shrunk, into two titanium plates.
93593.m: CHEOPS carries children’s drawings into space.

93594.q: According to CHEOPS measurements, what shape is the planet WASP-103b?
93594.e: WASP-103b orbits very close to its star. The strong tidal forces stretch it out like a rugby ball.
93594.m: An exoplanet can be stretched by tidal forces.

93595.q: Which organisation runs CHEOPS together with Switzerland?
93595.e: CHEOPS is a mission of the European Space Agency ESA. Switzerland is its most important partner in it.
93595.m: CHEOPS is an ESA mission with Switzerland.

93596.q: At roughly what height does CHEOPS orbit the Earth?
93596.e: CHEOPS flies over the poles at a height of about 700 km. This keeps the Sun at about the same angle to the satellite all the time.
93596.m: CHEOPS orbits at a height of about 700 km.

93597.q: What did CHEOPS discover in 2023 around the dwarf planet Quaoar, far out in the Solar System?
93597.e: When Quaoar passed in front of a star, CHEOPS helped to detect a ring. A ring so far from the dwarf planet surprised the researchers.
93597.m: The dwarf planet Quaoar has a ring too.

93598.q: Which university did the Swiss company ClearSpace come from?
93598.e: ClearSpace was founded in 2018 as a spin-off of EPFL, the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne. The company wants to collect space junk.
93598.m: ClearSpace comes from EPFL in Lausanne.

93599.q: What is the aim of the company ClearSpace?
a: To build rockets for the Moon
93599.e: ClearSpace is developing satellites that catch old objects in space. This is meant to make orbits cleaner.
93599.m: ClearSpace wants to clear junk out of space.

93600.q: How is the ClearSpace-1 satellite meant to catch a piece of junk?
93600.e: ClearSpace-1 has four gripping arms like a claw. It closes around the object and holds it tight.
93600.m: ClearSpace-1 grabs junk with gripping arms.

93601.q: What happens to ClearSpace-1 and the object it has caught at the end of the mission?
a: Both burn up in the atmosphere
Both stay in space for ever
93601.e: After the catch, ClearSpace-1 steers the pair into the atmosphere. There both of them burn up.
93601.m: ClearSpace-1 burns up together with the junk.

93602.q: With which organisation did ClearSpace sign a contract for the ClearSpace-1 mission in 2020?
93602.e: In 2020 the European Space Agency ESA ordered the mission for about 86 million euros. It is meant to be the first mission of its kind.

93603.q: Why did ClearSpace-1 need a new target in 2024?
a: The old target was probably hit by other junk
The old target landed on the Moon
The old target was too small to see
93603.e: The rocket adapter Vespa was the first target. In 2023 it was probably hit by debris and broke apart.
93603.m: Space junk can even destroy the target of a clean-up mission.

93604.q: According to the new plans, what is ClearSpace-1 meant to catch?
a: An old ESA satellite that no longer works
93604.e: The new target is PROBA-1, a small ESA satellite launched in 2001. It no longer works and is now space junk.
93604.m: ClearSpace-1 is meant to catch an old ESA satellite.

93605.q: Why is it difficult to catch a piece of junk in space?
a: It sends no signal and may be tumbling
93605.e: A dead satellite does not help. It does not send radio signals and may be spinning, so the catcher has to navigate very precisely.
93605.m: Junk in space does not help you catch it.

93606.q: On which planet does the Perseverance rover drive?
93606.e: Perseverance is a NASA rover. It has been exploring the surface of Mars since 2021.

93607.q: What was there long ago in the crater where Perseverance landed in 2021?
93607.e: Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater. Billions of years ago there was a lake there with a river delta.
93607.m: Perseverance landed in an old lake basin.

93609.e: Perseverance weighs about 1,025 kg and is roughly the size of a small car.
93609.m: Perseverance is about as heavy as a small car.

93610.q: What did the MOXIE experiment on Perseverance make from the Martian air?
93610.e: The air on Mars is mostly carbon dioxide. MOXIE split it and got oxygen from it.
93610.m: Oxygen has been made from the air on Mars.

93611.q: What is Perseverance mainly looking for on Mars?
93611.e: Perseverance studies rock from an old lake basin. Traces of tiny living things could have been preserved there.
93611.m: Perseverance is looking for signs of past life.

93612.q: What does Perseverance do with selected rock samples?
a: It fills them into small tubes
93612.e: Perseverance drills into rock and seals it in tubes. The samples may be brought to Earth later.
93612.m: Perseverance collects rock samples in tubes.

a: Keeping going and not giving up
93614.e: A school pupil from the USA suggested the name in a competition. Perseverance means sticking at something and not giving up.

93615.q: Which famous space telescope is seen as the predecessor of the James Webb telescope?
